cards.title: PEP 8: The Style Guide That Removes a Class of Arguments
cards.teaser: PEP 8 is Python's official style guide — not an opinion, but a shared contract that lets teams argue about logic instead of formatting. Consistent style makes code readable by anyone who knows Python, not just the person who wrote it.

runs.text: (Python Enhancement Proposal 8, authored by Guido van Rossum and Barry Warsaw) specifies how Python code should be formatted. It covers indentation (4 spaces, never tabs), line length (79 characters for code, 72 for docstrings), blank lines between functions and classes, import ordering, naming conventions, and whitespace around operators.
The most important naming conventions from PEP 8:

runs.text: Why does this matter? Because the cost of inconsistent style compounds over a project's lifetime. A developer reading code formatted consistently can build intuition; one reading mixed styles must parse the format before parsing the logic. Guido's insight is captured in the PEP 8 preamble: code is read far more often than it is written.
reformats code to a strict PEP 8–compatible subset without negotiation;
does both at Rust speed. Running any of these in CI ends style debates permanently — the tool decides, not the team.

PEP 8 includes one explicit exception: "A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds" (Emerson). It acknowledges that local context sometimes justifies deviation. The key word is intentional — you deviate because you have a reason, not because you forgot the rule.

PEP 8 is Python's formatting rulebook. Following it means any Python developer can read your code without first learning your personal style preferences. Automate enforcement with a linter and never think about it again.

cards.title: The Walrus Operator: Assignment Inside Expressions
cards.teaser: The walrus operator (:=) assigns a value and returns it in a single expression, eliminating the redundant read-assign-use pattern and making code that was previously spread across multiple lines fit cleanly into a condition or comprehension.

The classic case it eliminates: computing a value, checking if it's valid, then using it. Without

The walrus operator is particularly valuable in
loops that consume data until exhausted — the "read chunk, process if non-empty" pattern that previously required duplicating the read call or using

when it genuinely eliminates repetition or clarifies intent. Avoid it when it makes a simple assignment harder to spot — walrus in deeply nested comprehensions often harms readability more than it helps.

The parentheses in if (n := len(a)) > 10: are required when the walrus expression is part of a larger comparison. Without them, the parser reads := as having lower precedence than > and raises a SyntaxError.
The walrus operator lets you assign a variable and use its value in the same expression — particularly useful in while loops and if conditions where you'd otherwise compute the same thing twice.

cards.title: Unpacking: Structured Assignment Without Indexing
cards.teaser: Unpacking assigns multiple variables from any iterable in a single statement, replacing error-prone index-based access with named, readable targets. Extended unpacking with a starred expression makes it work for sequences of arbitrary length.

Unpacking removes the most common source of magic numbers in Python code — index-based access into sequences whose structure is known. Replacing

If the number of values does not match the number of targets (and no starred expression is present), Python raises ValueError: too many values to unpack or not enough values to unpack. This is a feature — unpacking is self-documenting about expected structure.
Unpacking lets you name the parts of a sequence in one assignment instead of indexing into it repeatedly. The starred expression handles the leftovers when the sequence length isn't fixed.

cards.title: enumerate() Instead of range(len())
cards.teaser: enumerate() gives you both the index and the value from any iterable in a single, readable loop — replacing the brittle range(len(items)) pattern that forces manual indexing and makes off-by-one errors easy to introduce.

cards.title: zip() for Parallel Iteration
cards.teaser: zip() pairs elements from two or more iterables into tuples, letting you iterate over multiple sequences in lockstep without managing indexes — and zip_longest() handles the case where the sequences aren't the same length.

runs.text: is a built-in that takes two or more iterables and produces tuples pairing their elements at the same position. It replaces the index-synchronized loop pattern —
for i in range(len(names)): process(names[i], scores[i])
for name, score in zip(names, scores):

zip() lets you iterate over two or more lists in parallel, giving you matching elements as tuples — no index math required. Use strict=True (Python 3.10+) if the lists should be the same length.

cards.title: List Slicing Idioms
cards.teaser: Python's slice syntax is expressive enough to express most sequence-manipulation patterns without manual index arithmetic — and its edge-case-safe defaults (omitting start or stop) make boundary conditions free.

cards.title: any() and all() for Boolean Aggregation
cards.teaser: any() and all() express boolean aggregation over iterables in a single readable call — replacing explicit loops that accumulate a flag, and short-circuiting as soon as the result is determined.

The idiom works best when combined with a generator expression, so the condition is evaluated lazily:

items.text: — returns True as soon as it finds a score above 90
— returns False as soon as it finds an inactive user
— equivalent to bool(errors) for a list, but works on any iterable

runs.text: , the equivalent requires a flag variable and an early-exit pattern:
found = False; for x in items: if condition(x): found = True; break
. The built-in collapses this pattern to a single expression, which composes naturally with

any() says "is at least one of these true?" and all() says "are all of these true?" Both work on any iterable, both short-circuit, and both replace explicit flag loops with a single readable expression.

cards.title: f-strings: Formatting as a First-Class Citizen
cards.teaser: f-strings (formatted string literals) embed arbitrary Python expressions directly inside string literals, making most formatting tasks readable in a single line — and replacing the older % formatting and .format() patterns that separated values from their template.

runs.text: Python has three generations of string formatting, each a response to the previous one's limitations:

items.text: . Error-prone when the number of arguments doesn't match the format string; becomes unreadable with many substitutions.
. Supports positional and named references, but still separates the values from their position in the template.
. Values appear exactly where they are used. Any Python expression is valid inside the braces.

runs.text: f-strings support the full Python format mini-language inside the braces.
formats a float to two decimal places.

remains necessary is when the format string is stored separately from the values — for example, in a configuration file or a translation table — because f-strings are evaluated at definition time and cannot be deferred.

f-strings are faster than both % formatting and .format() at runtime because they are evaluated as Python expressions by the interpreter rather than parsed at call time. For hot loops, the performance difference is measurable.
f-strings put the variable right where it's used in the string, inside curly braces. Any Python expression works inside the braces, and format specifiers control how the value is displayed.

cards.teaser: is tests whether two names point to the exact same object in memory; == tests whether two objects have the same value. Confusing them produces bugs that are nearly invisible — especially with integers, strings, and None.

== asks "do these have the same value?"; is asks "are these literally the same object in memory?". Use is only for None, and let == handle everything else.

cards.title: Comprehensions: Expressive Data Transformation
cards.teaser: List, dict, and set comprehensions express data transformation in a single readable expression — filtering and mapping a collection without a for loop, a temporary variable, or an explicit append. They are faster than the equivalent loop in CPython.

runs.text: Python comprehensions come in three forms:

items.text: [expr for item in iterable if condition]
{key_expr: value_expr for item in iterable if condition}
{expr for item in iterable if condition}

runs.text: clause is optional — omit it to transform every element. The expression part can be any Python expression. Comprehensions replace the
result = []; for item in iterable: if condition: result.append(transform(item))
pattern with one line that is semantically equivalent and typically 10-40% faster due to CPython's internal optimization of the comprehension bytecode.

Comprehensions become unreadable when they exceed roughly two conditions or two nested loops. Slatkin's rule: if a comprehension spans more than two lines when formatted with PEP 8 line limits, replace it with a regular for loop. Clarity beats cleverness.
When memory is a concern, use a
instead — the same syntax with parentheses:
. It produces values lazily without building the full list in memory. This is especially important when the result is consumed by another function:
There is no tuple comprehension — (expr for x in iterable) is a generator expression, not a tuple. Use tuple([expr for x in iterable]) or tuple(expr for x in iterable) if a tuple is required.

Comprehensions are a one-line way to build a transformed list, dict, or set from any iterable — filter and transform in a single readable expression. Keep them simple; when they get complex, switch back to a plain for loop.

cards.title: EAFP vs LBYL: Two Philosophies of Error Handling
cards.teaser: EAFP (Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission) uses try/except to attempt an operation and handle failures; LBYL (Look Before You Leap) checks preconditions before acting. Python's idioms favor EAFP — it is faster, race-condition-safe, and avoids redundant checks.

runs.text: These two philosophies describe how code deals with conditions that might prevent an operation from succeeding:

items.text: (Look Before You Leap) checks whether an operation will succeed before attempting it:
if key in d: return d[key]
. Common in C, Java, and statically typed languages where exceptions are expensive.
(Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission) attempts the operation and handles failure:
try: return d[key] except KeyError: return default
. Python's duck typing, dynamic dispatch, and cheap exceptions make this the idiomatic style.

runs.text: EAFP has three concrete advantages in Python:

items.text: In LBYL, the state checked may change between the check and the operation (a file deleted between
). EAFP operates on the current state — the exception reflects what actually happened.
LBYL checks and then accesses; EAFP just accesses. In the happy path, EAFP is one operation instead of two.
checks that reject valid duck-typed alternatives. EAFP lets any object that supports the operation succeed.

runs.text: LBYL is appropriate when the check is cheap and the failure path is truly exceptional — for example, validating user input before processing a long pipeline. The choice is about communicating intent:
communicates "this is the normal path, absence is the exception."

Python's standard library leans EAFP. dict.get(key, default), collections.defaultdict, and contextlib.suppress() all encode EAFP patterns. When the standard library offers a built-in for a common EAFP case, prefer it over explicit try/except.
LBYL checks first, then acts. EAFP acts first, then handles failure. Python favors EAFP because exceptions are cheap and pre-checks can be wrong by the time the action runs.
